generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up in the small habits of a field: how a claim is phrased, how cautious a conclusion is allowed to be, and what counts as enough evidence to make a point. Across disciplines these habits differ, and much of the time no one states them openly. You absorb them from the writing you read and the feedback you receive, rather than from a rulebook. Noticing them, and writing towards them, is how your work starts to read as the work of someone inside the subject.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students making the same point, that a result should be read with caution, for an assignment in their subject.

{{learner-a}} writes it the way it would be written in any subject: 'I think this result is quite interesting, but I am not sure we can fully trust it.' The point is there, but the register is generic and personal. In a field that expects claims to be tied to evidence and the writer kept in the background, it reads as informal and unsupported, whatever its merits.

{{learner-b}} writes the same caution in the conventions of the field: 'The effect is sizeable, but its basis in a single setting limits how far it can be generalised.' The judgement is identical. What differs is that {{learner-b}} has adopted the field's vocabulary, its restraint, and its habit of grounding a claim in a specific limitation. It reads as the work of someone inside the subject.

Both students reached the same judgement. Only {{learner-b}} expressed it in the conventions the subject is marked against.
generatedProse.summary: Academic writing is not one skill but many, each situated in a discipline that sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure. You can now explain why there is no monolithic academic writing, analyse how two fields differ, and begin to identify the conventions of your own. The next lesson turns recognition into method: how to work those conventions out from the writing your discipline already publishes.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s version read as writing from inside the subject rather than generic?

items.text: It adopted the field's vocabulary and restraint and grounded the claim in a specific limitation.
It reached a more cautious judgement than {{learner-a}}'s.
It was longer and used more words.
It avoided citing any evidence at all.

feedback.correct: That's right. Same judgement, expressed in the conventions the subject is marked against and tied to a specific limitation.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. The two judgements were the same; look at how {{learner-b}} expressed theirs.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s version read as disciplinary because it adopted the field's vocabulary and restraint and tied the claim to a specific limitation, not because it was longer or more cautious.
